card.title: Predict the order law without the server
card.plain: Every chunk is stamped by the first ticket that reaches it, within three chunks. Two build orders give the same world when those stamps agree around the chunks we look at. This one rule, written down before any measurement, says a 2x2 square has 4 worlds, a line of 3 has 3, a line of 4 has 8, and that order stops mattering once tickets are 5 chunks apart.
card.why: The rule has one dial (three chunks, from the earlier tile measurement), and the line of 4 reads it: 12 worlds if the dial is 2, 8 if 3, 4 if 4. It already matches the 4 worlds of the square measured earlier, and it runs in seconds.
card.done_when: The script returns 4 worlds of 6 orders for the square, 3 for the line of 3 and the triangle, 8 for the line of 4, and 4,4,20,20,1,1,1 for squares spaced 1 to 7 chunks apart.

card.title: Test the law with 85 server starts, not 214
card.plain: Build one world for each predicted class, one repeat as a control and one extra order from the biggest class. All the worlds are then compared with each other on disk, which costs no server start.
card.why: Trying every order plus a control takes 214 starts, about 71 minutes on two servers. The class plan takes 85, about 28 minutes. At spacing 3 and 4 it saves only 3 of 25, and the plan says so.
card.done_when: The plan counts 5, 5 and 10 starts for the line of 3, the triangle and the line of 4, 6,6,22,22,3,3,3 for the seven squares, and 85 in all against 214.

card.title: Pick the build order that gives the most ore
card.plain: Given the table of worlds, choose the one with the most of an ore in a chosen chunk, and say if it is the only best one. On the measured square, iron in chunk (64,64) is 149 only when the first chunk built is (64,65). Diamonds are the same in all four worlds, so for diamonds the answer is no move.
card.why: Four builds prove the best order, one per world. Searching the 24 orders needs all 24 to prove it, and about 3.6 builds just to stumble on it.
card.done_when: On the measured square the picker returns 149 iron for (64,64), says gold (16) is not unique and diamonds give no move, and counts 4 builds.

card.title: Price digging and swimming instead of remembering holes
card.plain: Digging through stone and swimming across water become prices on a step: a stone costs its digging time plus a step, water costs a swim price plus a step. One distance map per pickaxe level then replaces searching every map-and-backpack combination.
card.why: Four maps of at most 4096 cells (16,384 numbers) against up to 75.5 million map-and-backpack states. The swim price is a dial to be measured in the real game.
card.done_when: On a 4-cell strip with two stones the stone pickaxe costs 39 ticks to the end and the bare hand 315, and a strip with one water cell costs 15 with swimming and no route without.

card.title: Cross the islands on the real map
card.plain: On the real 64x64 spawn map of seed 7, no walking route reaches any iron from any of 1,417 starts because water and stone are walls. With digging and swimming priced, the same start is asked for a route to the iron.
card.why: It turns the finding that the real terrain is islands into a route, or into the proof that digging does not help.
card.done_when: From the spawn start with a stone pickaxe the map gives a number of ticks to the cell next to the nearest iron, or an honest none that is reported.

card.title: Predictions come first
card.plain: The test checks the saved history of the project: the file with our predictions must have been saved before any file with experiment results, and a made-up history where it was saved after must be rejected.
card.why: A prediction written after seeing the numbers is not a prediction.
card.done_when: Predictions are older than every result they are compared with, and a reversed or tied history fails.

card.title: Every setup repeats cleanly
card.plain: Each setup must have been run twice with the same order, and the two worlds must differ in zero blocks; a setup with no repeat or a differing repeat may not report how many kinds of world it found.
card.why: If the same order disagrees with itself, differences between orders cannot be believed.
card.done_when: A missing or differing repeat voids the count and a clean repeat lets it stand.

card.title: The window is inside the finished area
card.plain: Every chunk we compare must be close enough to a ticket to be fully built; a window with a corner too far from every ticket must be rejected.
card.why: Chunks outside the finished area are only partly saved, so comparing them would invent or hide differences.
card.done_when: All window chunks are within 2 chunks of a ticket in every setup, and the too-wide example fails.

card.title: Same world means the same everywhere
card.plain: If world a matches b and b matches c, then a must match c; a table of comparisons that breaks this, or disagrees with the saved fingerprints, is rejected.
card.why: Grouping orders into kinds of world only makes sense if matching is consistent.
card.done_when: No measured triple breaks the rule and made-up broken tables fail.

card.title: No Minecraft files in the repo
card.plain: The test looks at every file the repo would publish and rejects world saves, level files and server jars, and any result file over 2 MB.
card.why: Minecraft's files are not ours to publish and the repo should stay small.
card.done_when: A throwaway repo with such files fails and the real repo has none.

card.title: Route costs match the rulebook
card.plain: The new route model must charge the same time for walking, digging with each tool, crafting and smelting as the round 1 rules do.
card.why: A route is only comparable to round 1 if the same move costs the same.
card.done_when: Every round 1 move costs the same in the model and in the rules.

card.title: Waiting does not change the world
card.plain: Two touching tickets are built once with no wait and once with a one minute wait between them, and the saved blocks in their window must match.
card.why: If waiting changes the world, a count of kinds of world would count waiting schedules, not orders.
card.done_when: The two windows have zero differing blocks.

card.title: The law, written down first
card.plain: A short rule says how many different worlds a set of build orders can make, and the numbers it predicts are saved in the repo before any server run.
card.why: A prediction made after the answer proves nothing.
card.done_when: The law's counts match hand values and the predictions file is older than every result.

card.title: Four experiments against the prediction
card.plain: Each ticket layout is built on the real server in every order, and the number of different worlds is compared with the prediction.
card.why: This is where the law can be killed by one wrong number.
card.done_when: E1 to E4 each have a measured class count and a verdict next to the prediction.

card.title: How much order the world forgets
card.plain: The world keeps some facts about how it was built and drops others; we count the dropped information in bits and check that 'same world' behaves like a proper grouping.
card.why: This is the Godel-style quantity: what a finished world cannot say about its own history.
card.done_when: The bits lost are computed from measurements and equal the law's value.

card.title: Has anyone stated this law?
card.plain: A search of the Minecraft wiki, bug tracker and mathematics papers, with every source and its link kept in one file.
card.why: A law that already exists in a paper is not a discovery.
card.done_when: The file lists queries, links, and for each close hit what it does not say.

card.title: The shape of the real terrain
card.plain: Real seed 7 terrain is measured with persistent homology: at what price do separate regions join into one.
card.why: The round 2 map showed only islands; the joining price tells how much digging or swimming a route needs.
card.done_when: The joining price of start and iron equals an independent cheapest-bottleneck path.

card.title: Does it change the route?
card.plain: A planner that may dig through stone and swim at a price is raced against plain breadth-first search with the same number of steps allowed.
card.why: Round 2 found no route at all on real terrain, so the priced model decides whether routing is possible.
card.done_when: Equal budgets, a route where round 1 found none, and a stated effect of the build order on the route.

card.title: Round 3 on the website
card.plain: A round 3 page shows the goals, their status and each prediction beside its measurement.
card.why: The owner reads the result on the site, not in the repo.
card.done_when: site/r3.html loads r3.json and links from the main page.

card.title: E1, E2 and E3 against their predictions
card.plain: Three ticket layouts (a line of 3, the 2x2 square, a triangle) are built in every order and the count of different worlds is checked against the saved prediction.
card.why: The first three layouts decide whether the law survives.
card.done_when: E1, E2 and E3 each match their predicted count.

card.title: E4, repeat controls and the polytope identity
card.plain: The line of 4 is checked against its prediction, every repeat control must show no difference, and the counts are compared with the corners of a many-sided shape.
card.why: These checks make the counts trustworthy and tie them to known geometry.
card.done_when: E4 matches, all repeats are identical, and the polytope corners agree.

card.title: Route model and race
card.plain: A planner with dig and swim prices is built and raced against plain breadth-first search with equal step budgets.
card.why: The fair race is the base of every route claim.
card.done_when: Dig and swim cost on a hand map, the bottleneck bound, and equal budgets.

card.title: Real terrain and the player move
card.plain: On real seed 7 terrain the planner is compared with breadth-first search, a route is looked for, and the reach of the build-order move is stated.
card.why: This is where routing meets the real map and the order lever.
card.done_when: Planner not worse than BFS, a route exists, and the lever reach is stated.

card.title: Count worlds by brute force
card.plain: A small function tries every order of k tickets, treats pairs that cannot swap as fixed, and counts the different results.
card.why: It gives the law's number without any server.
card.done_when: Path of 3 gives 4, triangle 6, path of 4 gives 8, four mutually fixed gives 24, no fixed pairs gives 1.

card.title: A ticket on built ground does nothing
card.plain: If a ticket's chunk is already built by an earlier ticket it adds nothing, so only the first ticket of a close group matters.
card.why: This is what turns the 2x2 square's 24 orders into 4.
card.done_when: The square (all four within 2 chunks) gives 4 classes, one per first ticket.

card.title: Saved predictions equal the law
card.plain: The predictions file written by the simulator lane must give the same class counts as the brute-force function for E1, E3 and E4.
card.why: Two independent routes to the same number.
card.done_when: E1 4, E3 6, E4 8 in the file; E2 holds a whole number from 1 to 6.

card.title: Predictions came first
card.plain: The commit that adds the predictions file must be an ancestor of the commit that adds each experiment result.
card.why: This is the pre-registration, checked by git itself.
card.done_when: git says predictions are an ancestor of the E1, E2, E3 and E4 results.

card.title: E1: a line of 3 tickets 5 apart
card.plain: All orders of a line of 3 tickets 5 apart are built on the real server; the number of different worlds must equal the prediction (4).
card.why: Equal numbers support the law; a different number kills it and says which pair of tickets was misjudged.
card.done_when: Measured classes equal the saved prediction, and the grouping of orders matches too.

card.title: E2: the 2x2 square seen through the wide window
card.plain: All orders of the 2x2 square seen through the wide window are built on the real server; the number of different worlds must equal the prediction (5).
card.why: Equal numbers support the law; a different number kills it and says which pair of tickets was misjudged.
card.done_when: Measured classes equal the saved prediction, and the grouping of orders matches too.

card.title: E3: a triangle of 3 tickets 3 apart
card.plain: All orders of a triangle of 3 tickets 3 apart are built on the real server; the number of different worlds must equal the prediction (6).
card.why: Equal numbers support the law; a different number kills it and says which pair of tickets was misjudged.
card.done_when: Measured classes equal the saved prediction, and the grouping of orders matches too.

card.title: E4: a line of 4 tickets 5 apart
card.plain: All orders of a line of 4 tickets 5 apart are built on the real server; the number of different worlds must equal the prediction (8).
card.why: Equal numbers support the law; a different number kills it and says which pair of tickets was misjudged.
card.done_when: Measured classes equal the saved prediction, and the grouping of orders matches too.

card.title: Repeat controls are clean
card.plain: Every experiment repeats at least one order and the two copies must be identical block for block.
card.why: If a repeat differs, the differences are noise and no class count means anything.
card.done_when: All repeat controls show 0 differing blocks.

card.title: Bits lost, by formula
card.plain: The information lost is log2 of the number of orders divided by the number of worlds; the exact loss counts how many orders share each world.
card.why: This is the one number the Godel idea needs.
card.done_when: 24 orders in 4 worlds gives 2.585 bits; 6 orders in 4 worlds gives 0.585.

card.title: Bits lost, measured
card.plain: From each experiment's class sizes the bits lost are computed and must equal the value the law predicted.
card.why: The loss is a prediction too, not just a count.
card.done_when: Measured bits equal predicted bits for E1 to E4.

card.title: 'Same world' is a real grouping
card.plain: If A equals B and B equals C then A must equal C, checked on every measured triple of orders.
card.why: Without this the classes would not be well defined.
card.done_when: Zero violating triples in partitions.json.

card.title: A wider window can only split worlds
card.plain: Looking at more chunks can separate two worlds that looked equal but never join two that looked different.
card.why: So 'order does not matter' can be refuted by one block but never proven for every window.
card.done_when: Classes in the wide window are at least the classes in the narrow window for the same orders.

card.title: Ore moves in swaps
card.plain: Between the worlds of the square, iron and gold in chunk (64,64) change by equal and opposite amounts.
card.why: It shows what the lost information is made of: contested cells, not new material.
card.done_when: Iron plus gold is 163 in all four classes, diamonds stay 1.

card.title: Every source has a link and a query
card.plain: Each entry in the source file has the search words used, a web address and a one-line finding.
card.why: A claim of 'nobody noticed' must show where we looked.
card.done_when: Every entry has query, an https address and a finding.

card.title: The right places were searched
card.plain: The file covers the Minecraft wiki, the bug tracker, trace monoids, acyclic orientations, left regular bands and order-independent generation.
card.why: A missing family is a hole in the novelty claim.
card.done_when: All six families appear with at least one address each.

card.title: Closest prior work says what it lacks
card.plain: For each near hit the file states in one line what the law adds that the source does not say.
card.why: This is the honest edge of the novelty.
card.done_when: Every near hit has a non-empty 'lacks' line.

card.title: Persistence output is consistent
card.plain: At each price level the Euler number from the counts of cells equals components minus loops in the saved output.
card.why: A wrong persistence run would poison the route model.
card.done_when: All listed levels agree.

card.title: Joining price is the cheapest bottleneck
card.plain: The price at which the start region joins the iron region equals the cheapest path where the dearest step is as small as possible.
card.why: A known theorem ties persistence to routing; we check it on real terrain.
card.done_when: The persistence value equals an independent bottleneck search on the seed 7 grid.

card.title: Dig and swim prices
card.plain: A prototype lets a route dig through stone or swim water at a set price per step, on a tiny hand-made map.
card.why: Round 1 treated stone and water as walls, which made real terrain islands.
card.done_when: The hand map costs exactly the hand-computed total with one dig and one swim.

card.title: Route cost never beats the bottleneck
card.plain: A route's total price is at least its dearest single step, equal when the route is one cell wide.
card.why: This links the terrain measurement to the planner.
card.done_when: True on three hand maps.

card.title: Equal step budget
card.plain: In every row of the race both solvers are allowed the same number of expanded cells.
card.why: Otherwise the race is not fair.
card.done_when: Budget equal in every row.

card.title: Planner against breadth-first search
card.plain: At equal budget the planner's route price is never above the breadth-first route price.
card.why: This is the round 2 race, redone on a model where real terrain has routes.
card.done_when: In every row planner price <= BFS price, or BFS found none.

card.title: A route on real terrain
card.plain: The priced model finds a route from the spawn grid start to iron where round 1 found none from 1,417 starts.
card.why: The islands finding is either dissolved or confirmed.
card.done_when: At least one start has a route, with its price and step count recorded.

card.title: What the build order moves
card.plain: Across the four worlds of the square the order changes iron and gold in chunk (64,64) by 2 but changes diamonds by 0.
card.why: So the lever reaches iron, not diamonds, for route purposes.
card.done_when: Iron spread is 2, diamond spread is 0.

card.title: Merge the cards with status
card.plain: A script joins the round 3 cards with each goal's status, a missing goal being pending.
card.why: One file feeds the page.
card.done_when: build() returns every card with a status.

card.title: Numbers read from files
card.plain: The page numbers come from the result files on disk; a missing file shows 'not run', never 0.
card.why: A zero would look like a measurement.
card.done_when: Each missing file maps to 'not run'.

card.title: The round 3 page
card.plain: One page function draws a card per goal with title, plain text and status.
card.why: The owner reads the result here.
card.done_when: Every card has data-goal, title, plain and status.

card.title: Prediction beside measurement
card.plain: For each experiment the page shows the predicted class count and the measured one; colour marks only agree or disagree.
card.why: The law is judged in public.
card.done_when: Both numbers and a verdict appear for E1 to E4.

card.title: Status file
card.plain: A file maps every round 3 goal id to a status, exported by House after each report.
card.why: The page cannot show a status the harness has not set.
card.done_when: Every key is an N3 id and every value is a known status.

card.title: Link from the main page
card.plain: The main page gets one link to the round 3 page.
card.why: One door between the pages.
card.done_when: index.html contains a link to r3.html.

card.title: Count the corners of a shape
card.plain: The number of different worlds is also the number of corners of a certain many-sided shape (a hypergraphic polytope) built from the ticket layout; that count is compared with every measured class count.
card.why: If the corners match the measurements for all layouts, the law is a known geometric object seen in a new place.
card.done_when: Corner counts equal the measured classes for E1 to E4.
